name: FINTRAC compliance-programme kit for newly covered factors, financing/leasing entities and cheque cashers
buyer: Small independent equipment/auto lessors and financers, factoring firms, cheque-cashing shops
trigger: PCMLTFA amendments brought financing and leasing entities, factors and cheque cashers under FINTRAC. FINTRAC pages mark them 'new' (April or July 2025, sources conflict). A trade association says full compliance programme expected by 1 April 2026. Obligations: compliance programme, client ID, record keeping, reports (e.g. large cash, suspicious transactions).
existing: Competitor search run: generic AML platforms (SEON, Sumsub) aimed at fintech/payments; ReallyTrusted for realtors and mortgage brokers; CFLA association guidance. No product built for small lessors or cheque cashers found. Vehicle-finance dealer enforcement said to start 2026 (secondary source).
unchecked: Exact effective dates and the final regulation text; number of small covered entities; whether FINTRAC reporting interface (FWR) already satisfies the reporting part; penalties; whether the 100,000 CAD / vehicle scope pulls in car dealers who finance. Competitors in the dealer/lender back office unchecked. Overlaps with 'generic AML' exclusion, so the angle must be sector-specific records plus training.

first_check.duty: PCMLTFA regulations in force: factors, cheque cashers (treated as money services businesses) and financing/leasing entities must run a compliance program, with a compliance officer, written policies, a risk assessment, a written training program and an effectiveness review at least every 2 years. They must also identify clients, collect beneficial-ownership information and keep records. They must report suspicious and large cash transactions, and discrepancies (from 1 Oct 2025). Leasing scope: business-purpose property other than real estate, passenger vehicles, and property worth $100,000 or more, so car dealers who finance or lease in-house are covered. Effective dates: 1 Apr 2025 per CFLA, UCDA and law firms; FINTRAC's "Who must report" page marks the sectors new as of 10 Jul 2025. Full compliance was expected by 1 Apr 2026. Penalties: administrative monetary penalties; one source gives $1 to $1,000 per minor sector-specific violation, with failing to file a suspicious transaction report treated as far more serious. I did not verify the final penalty schedule.
first_check.market: Not found. I found no count of covered financing/leasing entities, factors or cheque cashers; CFLA's linked regulatory impact assessment was not opened. Cheque cashers could be counted by filtering FINTRAC's money services business registry (open data), which I did not do. Likely buyers include independent lessors (CFLA members), merchant-cash-advance and factoring firms, and the subset of used-car dealers who finance in-house (UCDA members). The size is unverified.
first_check.competitor: Dealer KYC: Dealertrack Canada identity verification plus an AML tool for sanctions and PEP screening; its AML page does not mention compliance programs, training or reporting, and says each dealer is responsible for its own compliance. Also AutoCorp AVA ID (an auditable identity-verification record), FraudFighter (ID checks, PEP screening, FINTRAC audits) and Patronscan ID scanners. Compliance program write-ups and reviews: MNP, Doane Grant Thornton and Substance Law (fixed-fee compliance programs, money-services focus). CFLA offers webinars and best-practice guides to members; UCDA offers FINTRAC guidance. FINTRAC's own reporting system covers report filing for free (from prior knowledge, not checked this session). I found no software built to run the whole compliance program for small lessors, factors or cheque cashers.
first_check.reason: The duty is real and in force under Canadian federal AML law (the PCMLTFA regulations). CFLA says the rules took effect on 1 April 2025 and full compliance was expected by 1 April 2026; FINTRAC's own list marks these sectors "new as of July 10, 2025". The ongoing work is recurring: KYC on every client, record keeping, reports, staff training and a program review every two years. The rush to meet the deadline has passed. Dealer KYC is already covered by Dealertrack (Equifax) and AutoCorp AVA ID; consultants (MNP, Doane Grant Thornton, Substance Law) and CFLA guides cover the program write-up. Cheque cashers fall under existing money-services rules, where vendors are already active. I found no single compliance-program software for small lessors or factors, so the gap is narrow. Market size was not found.

challenge_check.killer: No single killer found. Partial overlaps: Paays AML Check/ID Verifier (KYC and screening for financing/leasing firms); UCDA's dealer AML policy template, program guide and KPMG training; consultant program builds (Substance Law, MNP, KPMG); generic MSB AML platforms (iComply, SEON, Sumsub) for cheque cashers. Not checked: the regulation's estimate of how many businesses are affected, and the 1 April 2025 vs 10 July 2025 date conflict for cheque cashers. I ran 9 searches against a budget of 8.
challenge_check.reason: I found nothing that kills the idea, but the space is crowded. The duty is real: regulations published in the Canada Gazette on 26 March 2025 brought factors, cheque cashers and financing/leasing entities under the Act from 1 April 2025, with a softer outreach year that ended in April 2026. Point tools already exist: Paays AML Check/ID Verifier, aimed at financing and leasing firms, plus Dealertrack, AutoCorp and FraudFighter for dealers. UCDA gives dealers a policy template and program guide plus KPMG training; CFLA serves lessors. Substance Law, MNP and KPMG sell program builds. Cheque cashers are treated as money services businesses, which generic platforms like iComply already serve. None of these runs the whole program (risk assessment, records, training, two-year review) for small lessors or factors. Market size is unverified.
